focus_areas: FA-01: Chain verification & crypto (chain.go, policy/evaluate.go, types/types.go, resolver/did.go)
FA-02: MCP/A2A middleware & nonce (middleware/{mcp,a2a,binding,decode}.go, nonce/store.go, ratelimit.go)

findings.title: Raw Ed25519 private key printed to stdout in hex
findings.description: keygen() generates a 32-byte Ed25519 private key, converts it to hex at lines 12-14, and calls console.log(`Private key  : ${privHex}`) at line 23. Any shell history, CI log capture, terminal scroll-back, or pipe to a logging sink records the key in plaintext. No zeroization of privKey or privHex occurs after printing.
findings.exploit_scenario: Operator runs `drs keygen | tee /var/log/setup.log`. Log file now contains private key hex. Any user or process with read access to the log can extract the key and forge delegation receipts signed by that operator identity. On CI systems that capture stdout, the key is exposed to anyone with access to build logs.
findings.recommendation: Write the private key to a file path given as a CLI argument (default ~/.drs/signing.key with 0600 permissions), not to stdout. Print only the DID and public key to stdout. Zeroize privKey (fill(0)) after key derivation.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly observable: console.log of hex-encoded private key bytes is unambiguous sensitive-data disclosure.

findings.title: README documents nonce check order as 'before chain verification' — actual code is the opposite
findings.description: README.md line 176 states JTIs are checked 'before chain verification'. Actual execution order in mcpMiddleware and a2aMiddleware: (1) verify.Chain (full Ed25519 check), then (2) CheckNonceReplay only on a valid result. The code order is correct and secure; the documentation describes the insecure order. This misleads security auditors and integrators.
findings.exploit_scenario: A security auditor reads the README and concludes nonce checking is the first gate. They do not flag this as a concern. If the code were 'fixed' to match the documentation (nonces first), JTI pre-exhaustion attacks would become possible via invalid-signature requests.
findings.recommendation: Correct README.md line 176: 'chain signature verification runs first; JTIs are committed to the nonce store only after the signature is confirmed valid. This prevents JTI pre-exhaustion attacks.'
findings.confidence_reason: Directly verified: code order in mcp.go:64-71 is verify-then-nonce; README says nonce-then-verify.

findings.title: max_calls policy field is never enforced at runtime anywhere in the SDK or middleware
findings.description: The Policy interface JSDoc states max_calls is 'INFORMATIONAL ONLY'. checkPolicyAttenuation() enforces child <= parent at issuance, but no component — SDK, CLI, MCP client, MCP server middleware — checks actual call counts. drsMcpMiddleware receives VerificationResult carrying context.leaf_policy including max_calls, but neither reads nor counts it.
findings.exploit_scenario: A human grants consent for max_calls: 5 on a high-cost API. Nothing in drs-verify, drs-mcp-server, or the SDK counts or rejects calls beyond 5. The agent executes 500 calls before exp fires, violating consented policy.
findings.recommendation: (1) Add policy_warnings?: string[] to VerificationResult when leaf_policy.max_calls is set, alerting integrators. (2) Add enforceMaxCalls middleware option backed by LRU Map<jti, number>. (3) Document prominently in MCP server README with reference implementation.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly verified: Policy.MaxCalls type exists, CheckAttenuation enforces attenuation, but no runtime counter exists anywhere in the codebase.

findings.title: max_calls present in signed receipts and attenuated but never enforced at verification time
findings.description: types.Policy.MaxCalls at line 19 is a *uint64 carried in signed receipts. policy.Evaluate explicitly excludes max_calls enforcement with a comment at evaluate.go line 19-22. Attenuation is checked (child <= parent) but actual call count is never read. VerificationContext.LeafPolicy includes max_calls so integrators can enforce it, but there is no forcing function — a Valid: true response carries no indication whether max_calls was consulted.
findings.exploit_scenario: A delegation receipt specifies max_calls: 1 (single-use capability). DRS verifier returns Valid: true for every invocation within the delegation window. If the tool server does not implement call-count tracking, the agent can invoke the tool hundreds of times.
findings.recommendation: Include MaxCallsHint in VerificationContext when LeafPolicy.MaxCalls != nil. Add a warning log in Evaluate when max_calls is present but cannot be enforced. Document prominently in the API reference.
findings.confidence_reason: Explicitly documented in source as informational-only. Field is present in signed payload, attenuated correctly, but the verification pass produces no enforcement signal.

findings.title: Policy field enforcement is opt-in — absent args keys bypass all capability restrictions
findings.description: policy.Evaluate guards every check with a key-presence test: `if toolRaw, ok := args["tool"]; ok { ... }`. If the attacker-controlled invocation omits the key entirely, every enforcement block is skipped and the capability is granted unconditionally. This applies to allowed_tools (line 58), allowed_resources (line 71), allowed_data_classes (line 85), pii_access (line 40), and write_access (line 49). A delegation receipt restricting allowed_tools: ["web_search"] is completely bypassed by an invocation with args: {}.
findings.exploit_scenario: A chain restricts allowed_tools: ["read_db"] and write_access: false. Attacker-controlled agent signs invocation JWT with args: {} (no keys). policy.Evaluate iterates all guards, each if-ok test returns false, nothing is checked. Invocation passes Block D with no POLICY_VIOLATION. Tool server receives Valid: true and executes an arbitrary tool write.
findings.recommendation: Flip from opt-in to opt-out: when a policy field restricts access, the corresponding args key MUST be present. If allowed_tools has entries but args contains no 'tool' key, return error: 'tool not specified but policy restricts allowed_tools'. Same for allowed_resources and allowed_data_classes. Document explicitly that absent args for boolean flags (pii_access, write_access set to false) is safe.
findings.confidence_reason: Code trace confirmed: every enforcement block in evaluate.go has an if-ok guard that skips enforcement when the key is absent. The delegation receipt's restriction is not applied.

findings.title: Shape 2 MCP middleware does not enforce body-to-invocation binding check — signed args vs actual args never compared
findings.description: drsMcpMiddleware() sends only the decoded bundle JSON to drs-verify (line 152) without including the MCP tool-call parameters. No body field is sent, so the verifier cannot perform the RFC 8785 binding comparison between invocation.args and the actual tool arguments in message.params. result.binding is never checked. Contrast with Shape 1 (http.ts line 64-91) which passes request.body and rejects on binding !== 'match'.
findings.exploit_scenario: Malicious MCP client constructs a bundle where invocation.args = {tool: 'read_file', path: '/etc/passwd'} and attaches it to a tools/call request with params = {tool: 'write_file', path: '/etc/cron.d/backdoor', content: '...'}. Chain verifies as cryptographically valid. Shape 2 middleware returns verified: true. Tool server executes the write — a capability the bundle never authorized.
findings.recommendation: Extract message.params?.arguments and include as body field alongside bundle in the POST to drs-verify, mirroring Shape 1. Then check result.binding === 'match' and call failClosed('BINDING_MISMATCH') when not. This must occur before returning a verified result to the tool server.
findings.confidence_reason: Code comparison between http.ts (binding enforced) and middleware.ts (binding absent) is direct. The binding check gap is unambiguous.

findings.title: Unbounded io.ReadAll in MCPMiddleware/A2AMiddleware binding path — no body size cap
findings.description: checkRequestBinding (binding.go:34) calls io.ReadAll(r.Body) with no size limit. When integrators mount MCPMiddleware or A2AMiddleware on their own server, the middleware does not apply http.MaxBytesReader before reading the body. Contrast: the built-in /verify endpoint in main.go line 312 applies http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxBodyBytes) before decoding. The 10s ReadTimeout bounds time but not RAM — at 1 Gbps for 10s that is potentially 1.25 GB per connection buffered into heap.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker registers as a legitimate delegated agent and sends POST requests with 500 MB bodies to a Go tool server using MCPMiddleware with any bindingMode. Each request passes the per-IP rate limiter, runs verify.Chain on the small header bundle (passes), then io.ReadAll buffers 500 MB. Four concurrent connections consume 2 GB of server RAM. Tool server OOMs.
findings.recommendation: Add http.MaxBytesReader inside checkRequestBinding before io.ReadAll, using a configurable limit defaulting to 1 MiB (matching /verify). Expose MaxBodyBytes parameter on MCPMiddleware/A2AMiddleware so integrators can tune the limit.
findings.confidence_reason: main.go uses MaxBytesReader for /verify; binding.go does not for the middleware path. The asymmetry is unambiguous.

findings.title: Confused-deputy replay: tool_server binding is deployment-default-off with no startup warning
findings.description: Line 287: `if deps.ServerIdentity != "" && invocation.ToolServer != deps.ServerIdentity`. The check is skipped when SERVER_IDENTITY env var is not set (the default). In that configuration, invocation.tool_server in the attacker-controlled JWT is never read. A bundle signed for tool server A can be presented to tool server B and verify as valid. No startup warning is emitted when ServerIdentity is empty.
findings.exploit_scenario: Two tool servers behind the same DRS verifier, both without SERVER_IDENTITY configured. Agent's bundle authorizes filesystem access on server A. Attacker replays it to server B's data-export tool. invocation.tool_server may name server A but the verifier never checks it. Server B receives Valid: true and executes the export.
findings.recommendation: (1) Log a startup warning when ServerIdentity is empty. (2) Optionally treat empty invocation.tool_server in payload as MISSING_TOOL_SERVER when the verifier has a configured identity. (3) Document that running without SERVER_IDENTITY is only valid in single-server environments.
findings.confidence_reason: The conditional at line 287 is unambiguous: empty ServerIdentity fully disables the D4c check with no indication to operators.

findings.title: nil nonce.Checker silently disables replay protection with no log or warning
findings.description: CheckNonceReplay (decode.go:77-79) returns false (proceed) when the ns nonce.Checker argument is nil. An integrator calling middleware.MCPMiddleware(deps, nil, mode, handler) compiles without error and produces a handler with zero replay protection. No slog.Warn, no metric, no panic when ns == nil is detected. The nil-pass-through is not documented in the public MCPMiddleware or A2AMiddleware signatures.
findings.exploit_scenario: Integrator builds tool server with middleware.MCPMiddleware(deps, nil, 'enforced', handler), intending to add nonce store later. Attacker intercepts one valid signed bundle. Replay it repeatedly: chain verification passes (signature valid), CheckNonceReplay returns false (ns nil), tool is invoked unlimited times with a single stolen token.
findings.recommendation: Validate nonceStore is non-nil at construction time in MCPMiddleware/A2AMiddleware: panic('MCPMiddleware: nonceStore must not be nil'). If nil must remain valid for testing, emit slog.Warn and increment a disabled metric in CheckNonceReplay when ns == nil.
findings.confidence_reason: Code directly shows: if ns == nil { return false } with no logging. Compiles cleanly with nil argument.

findings.title: Bundle field type validation only checks property presence — receipts and invocation types not verified
findings.description: validateBundleObject() (lines 103-118) checks only that parsed object has receipts, invocation, and bundle_version via the in operator — not their types. A malformed bundle can pass {"bundle_version": null, "receipts": {}, "invocation": 42} and be cast as valid ChainBundle. In audit.ts, bundle.receipts is iterated with bundle.receipts[i]! and .split('.') called without confirming elements are strings.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker crafts {"bundle_version":"4.0","receipts":{"length":1,"0":{"not":"a jwt"}},"invocation":"bad"}. Type cast succeeds. The for-loop iterates one element and jwt.split('.') is called on an object, throwing a runtime TypeError exposing internal stack information. The malformed object is also forwarded to drs-verify, wasting verifier resources.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit type guards: Array.isArray(parsed.receipts), every element of receipts is a string, typeof parsed.invocation === 'string', parsed.bundle_version === '4.0'. Reject with DrsError('MALFORMED_BUNDLE') on any type failure.
findings.confidence_reason: Validation function directly verified: uses `in` operator only, no Array.isArray, no typeof checks. The malformed bundle path is unambiguous.

findings.title: O(n·m) policy attenuation in policy.rs not fixed — v2 algorithm defect persists in list field comparison
findings.description: The is_attenuated_subset() function for list-valued fields (allowed_tools, allowed_resources, allowed_data_classes) uses nested iteration: for each element in child list, scan parent list for a match. With n child elements and m parent elements, this is O(n·m) per attenuation check, called once per hop in the chain. At moderate load with 16-hop chains and large allowed_tools lists, this reproduces the v2 performance defect documented in CLAUDE.md (25 million comparisons/sec at moderate load).
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker submits a chain where each hop's allowed_tools list contains thousands of entries. The attenuation check at each hop performs O(n·m) work. A 16-hop chain with 1000-entry lists produces 16 * 1000 * 1000 = 16 million comparisons per request, consuming significant CPU before any caching benefit applies.
findings.recommendation: Replace nested iteration with a HashSet-based check: load parent list into a HashSet<&str> (O(m) build), then check each child element in O(1). Total: O(n+m) per call. Apply to all three list fields. Add a test verifying sub-millisecond attenuation for 1000-element lists.
findings.confidence_reason: Code read confirmed nested loop at policy.rs:173. CLAUDE.md explicitly flags O(n·m) as a v2 defect that must be fixed. The Rust implementation still has it.

findings.title: CheckAttenuation does not enforce child exp ≤ parent exp — temporal escalation via policy path unchecked
findings.description: policy.CheckAttenuation (lines 105-187) covers max_cost_usd, pii_access, write_access, max_calls, allowed_tools, allowed_resources, and allowed_data_classes. It has no handling for the exp field. The temporal attenuation check in chain.go lines 308-315 also misses the case: parent has exp, child omits exp. A child that omits exp while the parent has exp set claims an unbounded delegation lifetime — temporal escalation not caught anywhere.
findings.exploit_scenario: Parent delegation: exp: 1700000000 (far future). Child delegation: exp: null (no expiry). chain.go line 308: receipts[i].Exp != nil is false -> skip. CheckAttenuation: no exp handling -> skip. The child has no expiry despite the parent restricting it. If the attacker can get a fresh parent issued while keeping the child's nil-exp delegation permanently active, the child effectively never expires.
findings.recommendation: In chain.go, add: if receipts[i].Exp == nil && receipts[i-1].Exp != nil, return TEMPORAL_BOUNDS_VIOLATION — a child cannot omit an expiry that the parent has set. Add the same logic to CheckAttenuation for defence-in-depth.
findings.confidence_reason: Code trace confirmed: the attenuation check at line 308 only fires when both parent and child exp are non-nil. The nil-child + non-nil-parent case is unhandled.

findings.title: Invocation receipt has no temporal validity check — stale and far-future invocations accepted indefinitely
findings.description: Block E (lines 327-342) enforces nbf and exp on each delegation receipt. InvocationReceipt.Iat (types.go line 81) is never compared against current time. An invocation JWT signed with an arbitrarily old or far-future iat passes Block E without any staleness or clock-skew check. Combined with the 1-hour nonce store TTL, an invocation signed months ago against a still-valid delegation chain can be replayed once the nonce TTL has expired.
findings.exploit_scenario: Delegation chain with 30-day exp. Day 1: agent invokes tool; invocation receipt JWT captured. Day 25: chain still valid; nonce store TTL for the JTI has long expired. The captured invocation JWT is replayed — Iat is 24 days in the past, but neither Go nor Rust checks Iat against current time. Nonce store no longer holds the JTI. Replay passes all six blocks.
findings.recommendation: Add a staleness check: reject invocation if now - Iat > maxInvocationAge (suggested: 5 minutes for strict, configurable). Also enforce Iat <= now + clockSkewTolerance (prevent far-future invocations). Alternatively, add Nbf/Exp to InvocationReceipt and enforce them in Block E alongside delegation receipts.
findings.confidence_reason: Block E code confirmed: only iterates over receipts slice (delegation certs), not the invocation. InvocationReceipt.Iat is read at block B for presence but never compared to time.Now().

findings.title: Temporal attenuation gap: child sets exp to nil when parent has exp — child gains unbounded lifetime
findings.description: Lines 308-315 enforce: if both exp fields are non-nil, child.exp <= parent.exp. The check is skipped when either is nil. If the parent sets exp (restricting lifetime) but the child omits exp entirely, the guard `receipts[i].Exp != nil` is false and the check is skipped. The child then has an unbounded lifetime that was not explicitly granted. Rust core has the identical gap.
findings.exploit_scenario: Parent delegation: exp: 1700000000. Attacker controls second hop. Second hop omits exp field entirely. chain.go line 308: receipts[1].Exp != nil is false -> skip. Child now has no expiry despite the parent restricting it. The parent's EXPIRED check eventually fires for the parent receipt, but the child's nil exp means it could be used in a different chain context without temporal restriction.
findings.recommendation: Add check: if receipts[i].Exp == nil && receipts[i-1].Exp != nil, return TEMPORAL_BOUNDS_VIOLATION. A child cannot omit an expiry that the parent has explicitly set. Apply same fix to Rust core chain/verify.rs.
findings.confidence_reason: Code trace confirmed: the guard `receipts[i].Exp != nil && receipts[i-1].Exp != nil` is the only temporal attenuation check; the nil-child + non-nil-parent case falls through.

findings.title: X-DRS-Bundle header decoded without per-header size cap — pre-auth allocation of up to 750 KB per request
findings.description: decodeBundle (mcp.go:55, a2a.go:42) is called before any authentication on the raw header string. Go's http.Server MaxHeaderBytes default is 1 MiB for ALL headers combined, not per-header. An attacker can send a near-1 MiB X-DRS-Bundle header, triggering ~750 KB base64 decode + json.Unmarshal before any signature verification. At 100 RPS per-IP rate limit, this is 75 MB/s of pre-auth allocation from a single source IP.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker sends 100 concurrent requests/sec (per-IP limit) each with a near-1 MiB X-DRS-Bundle header containing a malformed bundle. Each request triggers decodeBundle allocation of ~750 KB, then fails with 400. At 10 ms average processing time: ~1000 concurrent allocations * 750 KB = ~750 MB of live allocations from a single IP before any crypto check.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit size cap before decodeBundle: if len(bundleHeader) > maxBundleHeaderBytes (e.g., 65536 bytes — sufficient for 16-hop chains with realistic JWT sizes), return 413 immediately. Set MaxHeaderBytes explicitly on the http.Server in main.go.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed: no size check on X-DRS-Bundle header value before base64 decode. main.go sets no MaxHeaderBytes override.

findings.title: getBit returns false (not-revoked) for out-of-range status list index — silent fail-open
findings.description: getBit at line 228 returns false without error when the requested index is out of range for the loaded status list bitstring. A receipt with a status list index beyond the end of the list is treated as not-revoked (valid) rather than triggering an error. This allows revoked receipts to appear valid if the status list is truncated, corrupted, or if the index was assigned after the last cache refresh.
findings.exploit_scenario: Status list cache holds a truncated bitstring (e.g., from a partial fetch). A revoked receipt has index 50000, but the cached list only covers indices 0-40000. getBit(50000) returns false (no bounds check). The receipt passes revocation check F as 'not revoked'. A revoked agent can continue to make valid-appearing invocations.
findings.recommendation: When the requested index is >= len(bitstring) * 8, return an error (not false). Propagate this error up through the revocation check to fail-closed: if the revocation status cannot be determined, treat as revoked. Log the out-of-range access as a warning.
findings.confidence_reason: Reported from code read at status.go:228 with description matching the fail-open behavior. Consistent with the status list partial-read concern in THREAT_MODEL.md T5.

findings.title: CLI verify command defaults to plain HTTP localhost — no TLS validation or URL scheme enforcement
findings.description: verify.ts line 29 defaults to 'http://localhost:8080' when DRS_VERIFY_URL is unset. VerifyClient constructor (line 25) accepts any URL without scheme validation. In non-loopback deployments where DRS_VERIFY_URL is set to an http:// URL, the full serialised bundle — all delegation receipt JWTs and the invocation receipt — is transmitted in cleartext. No server certificate pinning or CA-bundle override is available.
findings.exploit_scenario: Operator configures DRS_VERIFY_URL=http://drs-verify.internal:8080. Network-adjacent attacker performs MITM on internal HTTP traffic. Attacker reads all bundle contents: delegation chain topology, tool call arguments, timing. Attacker also serves a forged {"valid":true} response, accepting any chain.
findings.recommendation: (1) In VerifyClient constructor, validate that baseUrl uses https: scheme in non-localhost contexts; log a warning for http://localhost. (2) Add rejectUnauthorized flag (default true) for test environments. (3) In CLI verify command, warn when resolved baseUrl is plain HTTP and non-loopback.
findings.confidence_reason: Default value 'http://localhost:8080' and absence of scheme validation confirmed in source.

findings.title: Rust verify_chain has no depth cap equivalent to Go's maxChainDepth=16 — unbounded chain length allows DoS
findings.description: The Go layer enforces maxChainDepth = 16 in chain.go. The Rust core's verify_chain function processes receipts without a corresponding depth cap. An attacker who sends a chain bundle directly to a Rust-path consumer (e.g., the WASM-loaded verifier in the SDK or future native bindings) can submit arbitrarily deep chains, each hop requiring full Ed25519 verification and hash chain computation.
findings.exploit_scenario: An adversary sends a 10000-hop chain to a WASM-based verifier. The Rust verify_chain processes all hops sequentially. Each hop requires Ed25519 verification (~50 µs each), so 10000 hops = ~500 ms per request. At moderate concurrency, this saturates available CPU.
findings.recommendation: Add a max_depth constant to drs-core/src/chain/verify.rs (value: 16, matching the Go layer). Return Err(DrsError::ChainTooDeep) when receipts.len() > max_depth before beginning verification. Add a test confirming 17-hop chains are rejected.
findings.confidence_reason: Go layer has explicit maxChainDepth cap; Rust layer reported to lack equivalent from FA-07 scan.

findings.title: No temporal validity check on InvocationReceipt in Rust core — replay risk
findings.description: The Rust verify_chain does not check iat on InvocationReceipt against current time. This is the same defect as F-013 in the Go layer, present in both implementations. An invocation JWT with an arbitrarily old iat passes temporal validation in the Rust core without any staleness check.
findings.exploit_scenario: Same as F-013 but through the Rust WASM verification path. A stale invocation captured months ago is replayed through an SDK-side WASM verify call. The Rust core accepts it without checking iat against current time.
findings.recommendation: Add staleness check in Rust verify_chain: if now.unix_timestamp() - invocation.iat > MAX_INVOCATION_AGE_SECS (suggested: 300), return Err(DrsError::InvocationStale). Apply same fix as F-013 recommendation. Ensure clock is sourced from a non-manipulable source.
findings.confidence_reason: FA-07 scan confirmed no temporal validity check on InvocationReceipt in Rust core. Consistent with F-013 design gap.

findings.title: Unrecognized bindingMode string silently degrades to lenient — enforced deployments undermined by typos
findings.description: checkRequestBinding only explicitly checks for 'off' (line 29) and 'enforced' (lines 47, 57). Any other string — typos, case mismatches ('Enforced', 'ENFORCED') — falls through to lenient path: mismatches are logged but requests are not rejected. No validation of mode string at MCPMiddleware/A2AMiddleware construction time.
findings.exploit_scenario: Integrator sets DRS_BINDING_MODE=Enforced (capital E). The env var comparison is case-sensitive. Middleware silently runs in lenient mode. Attacker signs a policy-compliant args value and sends a different body. Tool executes the different body without binding enforcement.
findings.recommendation: Validate mode string at construction time in MCPMiddleware/A2AMiddleware. Return error (or panic) on unrecognized mode string. Export constants BindingModeOff, BindingModeLenient, BindingModeEnforced.
findings.confidence_reason: Code confirmed: only 'off' and 'enforced' string literals are checked; no construction-time validation exists.

findings.title: Rust policy evaluation silently skips enforcement when required arg fields absent — fail-open bypass
findings.description: The Rust policy evaluation function has the same opt-in pattern as the Go layer (F-005): enforcement blocks are guarded by field-presence checks. If attacker-controlled invocation args omit required fields (tool, resource, data_class), enforcement is skipped and the invocation passes. This affects both the Rust native path and the WASM-loaded SDK path.
findings.exploit_scenario: Same as F-005 but via the Rust verification path. A WASM-loaded verifier in the SDK receives an invocation with empty args. The Rust policy evaluator skips all enforcement checks. The SDK verify call returns success for an invocation that violated the policy.
findings.recommendation: Same fix as F-005 applied to Rust: if policy.allowed_tools is non-empty, the invocation args MUST contain a 'tool' key. Absent key when policy restricts the field returns Err(PolicyViolation). Apply to all list-typed policy fields.
findings.confidence_reason: FA-07 scan confirmed the same opt-in pattern as the Go evaluate.go. Cross-layer design defect.

findings.title: No recursion-depth guard for JCS canonicalization — deeply nested attacker-controlled JSON causes stack overflow
findings.description: The JCS canonicalization implementation recursively traverses JSON values. There is no depth limit on recursive calls. An attacker who can control JSON content (e.g., in invocation.args or a policy field) can submit deeply nested JSON (e.g., 10000 levels deep) that exhausts the call stack and causes a stack overflow panic in the Rust verifier or WASM instance.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker crafts an invocation JWT where args contains a deeply nested JSON object: {a: {a: {a: ... }}} 10000 levels deep. JCS canonicalization recurses 10000 levels, overflowing the Rust stack. The verifier process panics (Rust panic unwind or abort). If via WASM, the WASM instance traps and the SDK call throws an exception.
findings.recommendation: Add a depth counter to the recursive JCS traversal. Return Err(DrsError::JsonTooDeep) when depth > MAX_JCS_DEPTH (e.g., 64). This is a single-line change at the entry of the recursive function.
findings.confidence_reason: FA-07 scan confirmed no depth guard in JCS canonicalization. Stack overflow from deeply nested JSON is a well-known class in recursive JSON traversal.

findings.title: 16-hop did:web chains trigger up to 17 outbound HTTPS fetches per request — DoS via DID resolution latency
findings.description: Block C calls verifyJWTSignature once per receipt and once for the invocation — up to maxChainDepth+1 = 17 calls. For did:web DIDs, each unique uncached DID requires an outbound HTTPS fetch with 10s timeout. A 16-hop chain with 16 distinct did:web issuers (all uncached) incurs worst-case 16 * 10s = 160s latency per request, exceeding the server's 30s WriteTimeout. Under concurrent attack traffic, 16 simultaneous requests create 256 simultaneous HTTPS fetches to 256 attacker-controlled endpoints.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker controls 16 domains each serving a DID document with 9.9s response delay. 10 concurrent /verify requests create 160 open HTTPS connections. After the 30s WriteTimeout kills the client connection, the singleflight context cancels the fetches — but the overhead of 160 TLS handshakes to attacker-controlled hosts on each burst is significant.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-request DID resolution budget: if total did:web resolutions attempted within one Chain() call exceeds N (e.g., 4), short-circuit with CHAIN_TOO_MANY_DID_FETCHES. Alternatively, provide a verifier policy flag requiring did:key only for strict latency deployments.
findings.confidence_reason: Code trace confirmed: Block C iterates all receipts without a separate did:web count limit. The circuit breaker only limits repeated calls to the same DID, not the total count of distinct did:web resolutions per request.

findings.title: did:web DID document extraction has no verification method id binding — attacker-controlled document injects chosen key
findings.description: extractEd25519FromDIDDocument (line 580) returns the first successfully parsed Ed25519 or JsonWebKey2020 entry without checking that the returned key corresponds to the DID's fragment (#key-1 etc). An attacker controlling a did:web endpoint can position an invalid entry before their chosen key, causing extractEd25519 to skip the first and return the attacker's key for signature verification.
findings.exploit_scenario: Compromised CDN serves did:web:corp.example.com DID document. Attacker inserts an Ed25519VerificationKey2020 entry with a corrupted multibase prefix (triggers continue), followed by their JsonWebKey2020 with their own key. extractEd25519FromDIDDocument returns the attacker's key. Signature verification accepts attacker-signed receipts as valid for corp.example.com.
findings.recommendation: When the DID has a fragment (did:web:corp.example.com#key-1), only extract the verification method whose id matches the fragment. When no fragment is specified, continue with first-match. This is the correct W3C DID Core document processing rule.
findings.confidence_reason: Code read confirmed: no fragment-based filtering in extractEd25519FromDIDDocument. The function returns first-match regardless of id field.

findings.title: In-memory nonce store exhaustion returns 503 for all valid requests — attacker with valid credentials can lock out all agents
findings.description: nonce.Store.Check returns ErrStoreExhausted when at capacity and no expired entries exist. CheckNonceReplay maps this to HTTP 503. Default: NONCE_STORE_MAX_ENTRIES=100000, NONCE_STORE_TTL=3600s. An attacker with valid signed bundles (legitimate delegated agent) can exhaust the store at 100 RPS per IP in ~16 minutes; with 10 IPs at the global 1000 RPS limit, in 100 seconds. All subsequent valid requests from all agents return 503 for up to 1 hour.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker controls 10 agent identities with valid signed bundles. Each generates fresh unique JTIs at 100 RPS (per-IP limit). After 100 seconds at global limit, store exhausted. For the next 3600 seconds, no new valid invocation from any agent on the platform can proceed.
findings.recommendation: (1) On exhaustion, evict oldest entries (LRU policy) rather than returning 503. (2) Document the exhaustion scenario as a configuration risk. (3) Recommend Redis backend (no capacity cap) for production multi-agent deployments.
findings.confidence_reason: ErrStoreExhausted path confirmed in store.go. LRU eviction only removes expired entries, not oldest non-expired. Capacity math is straightforward.

findings.title: Singleflight panic: done channel and inflight map entry not cleaned up in defer — goroutine leak on panic
findings.description: The singleflight implementation at lines 356-366 closes done channel and deletes the inflight map entry outside of a defer statement. If resolveUncached panics between acquiring the inflight entry and the cleanup code, the channel is never closed and the map entry is never removed. Subsequent goroutines waiting on the same DID block forever on <-e.done, leaking goroutines.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker triggers a panic in resolveUncached by crafting a DID document that causes a nil pointer dereference in the parsing code. The inflight entry is never cleaned up. Subsequent requests for the same DID hang indefinitely waiting on the closed channel. Goroutine leak accumulates until the server OOMs.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the cleanup in a defer: defer func() { close(e.done); r.mu.Lock(); delete(r.inflight, did); r.mu.Unlock() }(). Also use recover() to catch panics in resolveUncached and convert them to errors before propagating.
findings.confidence_reason: Code structure confirmed: cleanup code is sequential, not in defer. Panic in resolveUncached would leave the inflight entry and done channel in inconsistent state.

findings.title: TSA URL accepted without scheme or host validation — SSRF via attacker-controlled TSA endpoint
findings.description: The TSA URL (lines 149-154) is accepted from configuration or JWT payload without validating that it uses https: scheme or that the host is not a private/internal address. An attacker-controlled receipt can specify a TSA URL pointing to internal infrastructure (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data or http://internal-db:5432). The verifier will make an outbound HTTP request to the attacker-controlled URL.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker includes a DRS receipt with tsa_url: 'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data'. The verifier makes an outbound request to the EC2 metadata endpoint. The response is treated as a TSA response (likely fails to parse), but the request itself leaks that the verifier is running on EC2 and may expose metadata.
findings.recommendation: (1) Validate TSA URL scheme is https:. (2) Validate TSA host is not a private IP or loopback address (reuse the existing SSRF blocklist from the DID resolver). (3) Maintain a TSA allowlist: only URLs in TSA_ALLOWLIST are accepted. Reject receipts with out-of-allowlist TSA URLs.
findings.confidence_reason: TSA URL SSRF is a direct analogue of the did:web SSRF mitigated elsewhere in the codebase. No blocklist is applied to TSA URLs.

findings.title: WASM binary loaded without integrity verification — caller-supplied URL accepted without validation or hash pinning
findings.description: initWasm(wasmUrl?) performs a dynamic import and optionally initialises with a caller-supplied wasmUrl string at line 44. No SHA-256 or SHA-512 digest of the WASM binary is verified before instantiation. wasmUrl is passed directly to the wasm-pack init function without sanitisation or scheme restriction. A tampered module could return true for any bundle, bypassing all verification.
findings.exploit_scenario: Misconfigured deployment passes wasmUrl from env var WASM_BINARY_URL. Attacker with CI/CD access sets it to https://evil.example.com/fake_drs.wasm. Fake module exports verify_chain that always returns {valid:true}. All subsequent SDK verify calls return success regardless of bundle content.
findings.recommendation: (1) Pin expected WASM binary hash as a constant. After fetching, compute SHA-256 of bytes and compare before instantiation. (2) Restrict wasmUrl to https: scheme and allowlisted origins. (3) Document WASM path as not suitable for adversarial environments without a signed artifact with pinned hash.
findings.confidence_reason: No hash verification or URL restriction confirmed in loader.ts. The WASM binary is security-critical; lack of integrity check is a supply-chain risk.

findings.title: File-backed key management has no file permission check — world-readable key files silently accepted
findings.description: OperatorConfig defines operator_key_path as a plain path to a raw 32-byte Ed25519 signing key. validateOperatorConfig() at line 56 checks field presence but does not verify: file exists, permissions are 0600 or tighter, path is absolute, or that the file is not world-readable. Nothing zeroizes the Uint8Array after key derivation.
findings.exploit_scenario: Operator stores signing key at /home/operator/.drs/signing.key with permissions 0644 (common mistake). Config loads, key is read without permission check. Any local user on the same machine can read the 32-byte key and use it to issue arbitrary delegation receipts.
findings.recommendation: When operator_key_management === 'file', add permissions check: fs.statSync(operator_key_path).mode & 0o077 === 0 — reject with INVALID_OPERATOR_CONFIG if group- or world-readable. Validate absolute path. Zero-fill Uint8Array after key derivation. Consider using crypto.subtle with extractable: false.
findings.confidence_reason: validateOperatorConfig source confirmed: presence check only, no file system permission validation.

findings.title: Prefix wildcard lookup priority logic gap — specific rules may be shadowed by wildcards incorrectly
findings.description: The CapabilityIndex prefix wildcard lookup does not correctly prioritize specific rules over wildcard rules in all cases. An attacker-controlled capability request could match a less-restrictive wildcard entry instead of a more-restrictive specific entry, allowing broader access than intended.
findings.exploit_scenario: Policy grants access: specific rule: /tool/read_file -> allowed, wildcard rule: /tool/* -> denied. A request for /tool/read_file hits the wildcard first due to priority logic gap and is denied, or alternatively a less-specific wildcard that should be overridden by a specific deny is matched first, allowing access.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the lookup always returns the most-specific matching rule (longest prefix wins). Add comprehensive test cases for wildcard vs. specific rule priority. Verify with the capability index correctness tests referenced in Drs_language&algorithms.md.
findings.confidence_reason: FA-07 scan flagged priority logic gap. CapabilityIndex is security-critical; wildcard priority bugs directly affect capability enforcement.

findings.title: No dedicated rate limit on POST /admin/revoke — admin endpoint vulnerable to token brute-force
findings.description: The global rate limiter applies to all endpoints, but no dedicated per-endpoint rate limit or IP allowlist is applied specifically to /admin/revoke. An attacker who can reach this endpoint can attempt token enumeration at the global rate limit speed. While the token is compared via sha256.Sum256 (constant-time), the lack of lockout or dedicated throttle means brute-force at scale is limited only by the global bucket.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker sends requests to /admin/revoke at the global 1000 RPS rate limit, cycling through candidate tokens. Without a dedicated low-rate limit or IP allowlist on this endpoint, the attack surface is larger than necessary for a rare administrative operation.
findings.recommendation: Add a dedicated rate limiter for /admin/revoke: e.g., 10 RPS globally, 2 RPS per IP, with a 60-second lockout after 5 failures. Consider IP allowlist via ADMIN_ALLOWED_IPS env var, or mTLS authentication for the admin endpoint.
findings.confidence_reason: FA-04 scan confirmed no per-endpoint rate limit on /admin/revoke. Global rate limit is the only protection.

findings.title: TSA certificate validity checked against time.Now() instead of tst.GenTime — false rejections for archived receipts
findings.description: Certificate validity at lines 358-360 is checked against time.Now() rather than the timestamp token's GenTime. For archived receipts — where the TSA certificate has since expired — this produces false rejections even though the certificate was valid at signing time. RFC 3161 requires validating the certificate at the time of signing (GenTime), not the current time.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compliance audit requires validating a DRS receipt from 2 years ago. The TSA certificate used at signing time has since expired. The verifier rejects the receipt with a certificate validity error even though the timestamp was correctly issued. Audit evidence is falsely invalidated.
findings.recommendation: Replace time.Now() with tst.GenTime in certificate validity checks at lines 358-360. Add a test with a cert whose validity ended between signing time and verification time to confirm the correct behavior.
findings.confidence_reason: The RFC 3161 requirement to use GenTime for cert validation is unambiguous. FA-05 scan confirmed wall-clock usage.

findings.title: extractSignerCert matches by serial number only, not issuer — certificate substitution possible across CAs
findings.description: extractSignerCert at line 431 matches the signer certificate by serial number only. Serial numbers are only unique within a single CA; two different CAs can issue certificates with the same serial number. An attacker who can obtain a certificate from a CA in the trust pool with the same serial number as the TSA's signing cert can substitute it, potentially bypassing the signer verification.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker obtains a certificate from CA B (in the trust pool) with serial number matching the TSA's cert (signed by CA A). extractSignerCert returns the attacker's cert for signature verification. The TSA's signature is verified against the wrong certificate, producing a verification failure — but if the attacker can also forge the signature with their private key, the substitution enables a complete bypass.
findings.recommendation: Match on both serial number AND issuer: cert.SerialNumber.Cmp(signerInfo.IssuerAndSerial.SerialNumber) == 0 && cert.Issuer.String() == signerInfo.IssuerAndSerial.IssuerName.String(). This is the correct X.509 certificate matching per RFC 3161.
findings.confidence_reason: Serial-only matching is a well-known class of PKI vulnerability. FA-05 scan confirmed the implementation matches by serial only.

findings.title: strictVerifyEd25519 comment misrepresents Go 1.13+ behaviour — maintenance risk of future removal
findings.description: The comment at line 511-513 claims 'Go's stdlib accepts non-canonical S values'. Since Go 1.13, crypto/ed25519 already enforces S < L (canonical). strictVerifyEd25519 is defence-in-depth for cross-implementation parity with ed25519-dalek verify_strict, but the misleading comment could cause a future maintainer to remove it as redundant.
findings.exploit_scenario: Future maintainer reads comment, correctly observes Go 1.13+ handles this, removes strictVerifyEd25519 call. If linked against a future Go version that changes this behaviour, malleability protection is lost. TestStrictEd25519RejectsNonCanonicalS in chain_test.go does acknowledge this scenario.
findings.recommendation: Update comment: 'Go 1.13+ already enforces S < L; this check is defence-in-depth for cross-implementation parity with ed25519-dalek verify_strict and guards against future Go crypto changes. Do not remove.'
findings.confidence_reason: Documentation issue, no exploit path. Comment text confirmed misleading vs. current Go stdlib behaviour.

findings.title: Unverified parent JWT field values echoed verbatim into error messages — log injection risk
findings.description: issueSubDelegation() decodes parentJwt payload without signature verification (decodeJwtPayload is explicitly documented as 'Never use for verification'). The decoded parentPayload.aud and parentPayload.cmd values are embedded verbatim into DrsError message strings at lines 151 and 160. An attacker providing a crafted parentJwt can inject arbitrary strings (including newlines) into these error messages.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker passes a parentJwt whose decoded payload contains aud: 'legit-did\nFAKE_LOG_ENTRY: AUDIT PASS for mallory@evil.com'. The CHAIN_LINKAGE_ERROR message includes this verbatim. If forwarded to a SIEM as a single log line, the injected text appears as a separate audit event, polluting the audit trail.
findings.recommendation: Before embedding decoded JWT field values into error messages, strip control characters (\n, \r, \t) and truncate to 256 characters. For aud, validate it matches the DID format (did:key:z... or did:web:...) and replace non-matching values with '<invalid>'.
findings.confidence_reason: Log injection via unverified JWT field embedding is a plausible but low-severity concern. The error messages are not guaranteed to reach a log system.

findings.title: serde_json error messages in WASM output expose internal Rust type names and field paths
findings.description: When serde_json deserialization fails in the WASM-compiled Rust core, the error message includes internal Rust type names and field paths (e.g., 'missing field `issuer` at line 1 column 245'). These are surfaced through the WASM boundary to JavaScript callers. In production, this information can help an attacker map the internal JWT schema.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker sends malformed JWTs with random fields missing or mistyped. The error messages returned by the WASM verifier enumerate which fields are required and their exact Rust names, aiding schema discovery.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize error messages before crossing the WASM boundary. Map serde_json deserialization errors to generic 'MALFORMED_RECEIPT' errors without field-path details. Keep detailed errors only in debug builds (cfg!(debug_assertions)).
findings.confidence_reason: serde_json error messages containing field paths are a known pattern. The concern is real but the impact is information disclosure, not direct exploitation.

findings.title: JCS key sort uses JavaScript UTF-16 code unit order — diverges from RFC 8785 Unicode code point order for supplementary-plane characters
findings.description: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 requires object members sorted in ascending Unicode code point order. JavaScript Array.sort() sorts by UTF-16 code unit value. For supplementary-plane characters (U+10000+), UTF-16 surrogate pairs cause sort order to diverge from code-point order. This means a payload with supplementary-plane Unicode keys is canonicalized differently by this TypeScript implementation than by the Rust serde-json-canonicalizer, breaking cross-implementation hash agreement.
findings.exploit_scenario: A DRS payload contains a policy field key using a supplementary-plane character (emoji or CJK Extension B). TypeScript SDK computes a chain hash with a different JCS serialization than the Rust verifier expects. The Go/Rust verifier rejects the chain as hash-chain-broken — a correctness failure that can be misread as tampering.
findings.recommendation: Replace Object.keys(obj).sort() with a Unicode code-point comparator: sort((a,b) => { for each character index, compare codePointAt() values; advance by 2 for surrogate pairs }). Add a conformance test with a supplementary-plane key.
findings.confidence_reason: The RFC 8785 code-point vs UTF-16 unit distinction is real. Whether any real DRS payload uses supplementary-plane keys is unclear — hence confidence 0.75.

findings.title: JWT string split three times independently in same request path — maintenance risk
findings.description: The same JWT string is split by decodeJWTHeader (line 50), decodeJWTPayload (line 466), and verifyJWTSignature (line 496) independently. The re-join at line 501 (signingInput = parts[0] + '.' + parts[1]) reconstructs what was already computed. This is not exploitable but creates three independent parsing opportunities where a future refactor could introduce parsing inconsistency.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct exploit. Future refactor that breaks the split ordering or uses a different split count in one location could introduce a parsing inconsistency. Low-severity maintenance issue.
findings.recommendation: Refactor to a single parseJWT(jwt string) (header, payload, sigBytes []byte, err error) function used by all three call sites. Eliminates the three-times-split pattern and makes signing input construction unambiguous.
findings.confidence_reason: Code quality finding confirmed. No exploitable path in current code.

findings.title: trustProxy=true XFF rightmost-IP selection undocumented multi-hop limitation
findings.description: clientIP (lines 105-121) uses rightmost IP in X-Forwarded-For when TRUST_PROXY=true. This is correct for exactly one trusted proxy layer. With two proxy layers (CDN + load balancer), the rightmost entry is the CDN's egress IP, so all clients behind that CDN egress share a single per-IP rate bucket. No TRUST_PROXY_COUNT configuration exists.
findings.exploit_scenario: Operator deploys behind CDN with 5 egress IPs and sets TRUST_PROXY=true. clientIP returns CDN egress IP. All traffic through one CDN node shares a 100 RPS bucket. Attacker sending 100 RPS through that CDN node starves all other legitimate clients on the same CDN exit node.
findings.recommendation: Add TRUST_PROXY_COUNT config (default 1) implementing 'skip N rightmost' XFF logic. Add startup log warning clarifying the exact XFF semantic used. Consider supporting X-Real-IP for CDN deployments.
findings.confidence_reason: Multi-hop proxy XFF handling is a configuration concern rather than a code defect. Impact depends entirely on deployment topology.

findings.title: Timestamp verification failure is non-fatal — receipts without valid timestamps silently pass as if timestamped
findings.description: Timestamp failures in the verification path do not fail the chain. A receipt where VerifyTimestampTrusted returns an error is treated the same as a receipt with no timestamp at all — the chain is still returned as valid. Callers who rely on VerificationContext.TimestampTrusted to distinguish 'timestamp verified' from 'timestamp verification failed' may not check this field.
findings.exploit_scenario: An auditor queries for all receipts where TimestampTrusted: true to prove a capability was delegated before a specific deadline. A receipt with a tampered or missing timestamp still passes chain verification with TimestampTrusted: false — but if the auditor only checks Valid: true, the deadline proof is missing.
findings.recommendation: Add TimestampError field to VerificationContext indicating why timestamp verification failed. Optionally add a strict_timestamp mode that fails the chain if no valid RFC 3161 timestamp is present. Document clearly in API reference that Valid: true does not imply TimestampTrusted: true.
findings.confidence_reason: Design decision documented in code. The concern is that callers may not check TimestampTrusted. Real impact depends on auditor integration patterns.

findings.title: BundleProvider.getBundle() contract ambiguous — double-encoding risk if caller uses serialiseBundle()
findings.description: maybeInjectBundle() calls this.bundleProvider.getBundle() (line 68) which returns string | null, then passes the returned string to stringToBase64Url() at line 73. The interface documentation does not state whether the return value should be a raw JSON string or an already-encoded (base64url) string. If an integrator calls serialiseBundle(bundle) in their getBundle implementation, the result is double-base64url-encoded.
findings.exploit_scenario: Integrator writes: getBundle: async () => serialiseBundle(myBundle). The injected bundle is double-encoded. MCP server's base64UrlDecode returns a base64url string, JSON.parse fails, middleware returns MALFORMED_BUNDLE. Integration silently fails to inject bundles. Verification failures cannot be diagnosed without reading source of both packages.
findings.recommendation: Update BundleProvider interface JSDoc to explicitly state: return value must be a raw JSON string (JSON.stringify(bundle)). Alternatively, change interface to return ChainBundle (typed object) and move base64url encoding inside maybeInjectBundle(). Add a runtime check: if returned string does not start with '{', throw a descriptive error.
findings.confidence_reason: The contract ambiguity is real. Whether integrators would realistically make this mistake depends on API discoverability.

findings.title: Truncating cast u64 to i64 in unix_now() — incorrect timestamps for dates after year 2262
findings.description: unix_now() computes the current Unix timestamp as u64 then casts to i64. For dates after approximately year 2262, the u64 value exceeds i64::MAX and the cast truncates silently, producing a large negative timestamp. JWT temporal checks using this value will incorrectly evaluate all receipts as far-future or far-past.
findings.exploit_scenario: Not practically exploitable before year 2262. However, if tests use large synthetic timestamps to simulate far-future dates, the truncation causes test failures that mask real validation logic.
findings.recommendation: Use checked cast: i64::try_from(unix_timestamp).map_err(|_| DrsError::TimestampOverflow). Or use the time crate's i64-native UnixTimestamp type directly. Add a compile-time assertion that i64::MAX covers the designed validity period.
findings.confidence_reason: Integer overflow from u64->i64 is a real type-system issue. Impact is effectively zero until year 2262. Included for completeness.

findings.title: did:web path component not fully sanitized — potential path traversal in DID-to-URL mapping
findings.description: The did:web resolution maps DID components to URL path segments. If the path component contains encoded traversal sequences (%2F, %2E%2E) that are decoded before URL construction, an attacker-controlled DID could cause the resolver to fetch a URL on the target host that was not intended.
findings.exploit_scenario: DID: did:web:corp.example.com:path%2F..%2F..%2Fsecret resolves to https://corp.example.com/secret after path decoding. If the verifier's DID resolver trusts corp.example.com, this allows probing paths on the domain that were not intended to be DID documents.
findings.recommendation: Validate that each path component of the did:web DID, after percent-decoding, does not contain '/', '..', or other traversal sequences. Reject DIDs with invalid path components with INVALID_DID error before making any network request.
findings.confidence_reason: did:web path traversal is a known class. Whether this implementation decodes before validation requires code read confirmation.

findings.title: Duplicate DNS resolution for same did:web domain during concurrent cache misses
findings.description: The singleflight implementation coalesces inflight requests for the same DID, but DNS resolution for the underlying domain may occur multiple times if the system resolver caches are cold and multiple DIDs share the same domain. This is a minor efficiency concern rather than a security issue.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker submits a burst of requests with slightly different did:web DIDs on the same domain (did:web:corp.example.com:key1, did:web:corp.example.com:key2, etc.). Each DID gets its own singleflight group, triggering multiple DNS lookups for corp.example.com. Limited amplification effect.
findings.recommendation: Consider caching DNS resolutions at the resolver level or using a shared HTTP client with connection pooling. Low priority given the limited amplification.
findings.confidence_reason: Low severity. DNS caching behavior depends on system resolver configuration. Impact is negligible.

findings.title: Private IP blocklist for did:web SSRF protection may be missing some RFC 1918/6890 ranges
findings.description: The SSRF blocklist for did:web resolution covers common private ranges but may not cover all RFC 6890 Special-Purpose Address Registries (e.g., 100.64.0.0/10 Shared Address Space, 198.18.0.0/15 benchmarking, 240.0.0.0/4 reserved). An attacker with access to these ranges could potentially use them as SSRF targets.
findings.exploit_scenario: In a Kubernetes deployment, pod CIDR may use 100.64.0.0/10 (Shared Address Space). An attacker includes a did:web DID whose resolved IP falls in this range. If 100.64.0.0/10 is not blocked, the resolver fetches the DID document from an internal pod.
findings.recommendation: Audit the SSRF blocklist against the full RFC 6890 registry. Add: 100.64.0.0/10 (Shared Address Space), 198.18.0.0/15 (benchmarking), 240.0.0.0/4 (reserved), 0.0.0.0/8 (this network). Run the blocklist against a test suite of all RFC 6890 ranges.
findings.confidence_reason: Blocklist completeness depends on implementation. Low severity as most attack scenarios require unusual network configurations.

findings.title: Internal filesystem error details leaked in revocation store error messages
findings.description: Error messages from the FileBackedRevocationStore include operating system error details (file paths, errno values) that may be surfaced to API callers. These details expose the server's filesystem layout and can aid an attacker in understanding the deployment environment.
findings.exploit_scenario: A file permissions issue causes the revocation store read to fail. The error message 'open /var/drs/revocation/store.db: permission denied' is included in the HTTP response or log output visible to the API caller, revealing the server's filesystem path.
findings.recommendation: Wrap filesystem errors before surfacing them: return fmt.Errorf('revocation store unavailable: %w', sentinelErr) where sentinelErr does not include OS-level details. Log the full error internally with slog.Error. Return only generic error codes to callers.
findings.confidence_reason: Filesystem error leakage is a common pattern in Go error handling. The specific paths and error messages depend on implementation details not fully verified.

findings.title: No minimum token entropy enforcement on admin revocation token
findings.description: The admin revocation token is compared via sha256.Sum256 (constant-time) but no minimum entropy requirement is enforced. An operator could configure a low-entropy token like 'admin' or '12345', making brute-force trivially feasible even with the per-endpoint rate limit.
findings.exploit_scenario: Operator sets ADMIN_TOKEN=admin. Attacker brute-forces the token at 10 RPS (per-endpoint rate limit after fix). 'admin' is in the top 10 of common passwords and would be tried within seconds.
findings.recommendation: At startup, validate that ADMIN_TOKEN has at least 32 bytes of entropy (length >= 32 and passes basic entropy check). Reject startup with an error if the token is too weak. Log a warning if no token is configured.
findings.confidence_reason: Token entropy validation is missing per FA-04 scan. Impact depends on whether a per-endpoint rate limit (F-031) is applied first.

findings.title: http.Client Timeout shadows fetchTimeout context — timeout semantics may not behave as expected
findings.description: The status list fetcher uses both http.Client.Timeout and a context with fetchTimeout. When both are set, the shorter of the two fires first, but the error returned differs (context.DeadlineExceeded vs. url.Error with Timeout:true). Error handling that only checks for one form may not correctly handle the other, potentially leading to unexpected behavior in the error path.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct exploit. The error handling discrepancy could cause the fetcher to incorrectly retry or cache a partial result when the timeout fires via the http.Client path rather than the context path.
findings.recommendation: Use only the context deadline for timeout control and remove the http.Client.Timeout. Set the client Timeout to the same value as fetchTimeout for clarity, or set it to 0 (no client-level timeout) and rely entirely on the context.
findings.confidence_reason: Timeout shadowing is a subtle Go pattern issue. The actual impact depends on error handling code in the caller.

findings.title: FileBackedRevocationStore grows unboundedly — no size cap or rotation policy
findings.description: The FileBackedRevocationStore accumulates revoked receipt hashes without a size limit or rotation policy. In a long-running deployment with many revocations, the store file grows indefinitely. At sufficient scale, this could exhaust disk space and crash the server.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker with access to the /admin/revoke endpoint repeatedly revokes valid status-list indices. The FileBackedRevocationStore accumulates entries. Disk space is exhausted. The revocation server crashes and cannot be restarted until disk space is freed.
findings.recommendation: Add a maximum store size (REVOCATION_STORE_MAX_ENTRIES env var). Implement LRU eviction or compaction when the limit is reached. Log a warning when the store reaches 80% of the limit. Alternatively, migrate to the Redis-backed store for production.
findings.confidence_reason: Unbounded growth is a real operational concern for long-running deployments. Direct exploit requires access to the admin endpoint.

findings.title: Off-by-one read allocates up to 64 KiB + 1 bytes for unvalidated TSA response
findings.description: The TSA response reader may allocate 64 KiB + 1 bytes (off-by-one in the size check) before validating the response content. While the allocation size is bounded, the off-by-one means the intended 64 KiB limit is effectively 64 KiB + 1 bytes, which is a minor discrepancy from the documented limit.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker-controlled TSA endpoint sends exactly 65537 bytes. The reader allocates 65537 bytes before returning an error (too large). The extra byte allocation is negligible but represents a boundary condition that could be exploited in more constrained memory environments.
findings.recommendation: Fix the off-by-one in the size limit check: use > maxTSAResponseBytes (not >=) to ensure exactly maxTSAResponseBytes are accepted. Add a test case with exactly maxTSAResponseBytes and maxTSAResponseBytes+1.
findings.confidence_reason: Off-by-one boundary condition. Low severity — 1 extra byte is not materially exploitable.

findings.title: serde_json_canonicalizer pinned to '0.2' — may lag RFC 8785 conformance updates
findings.description: The serde_json_canonicalizer dependency is pinned to version '0.2' (minor version only). If the crate releases conformance fixes or new test vectors under '0.2.x' patch versions, the project may or may not pick them up depending on Cargo.lock state. More importantly, if RFC 8785 conformance updates require a major version bump, this dependency will not automatically track them.
findings.exploit_scenario: A conformance bug is found in serde_json_canonicalizer 0.2.x and fixed in 0.3.0. DRS continues using 0.2.x. Canonicalization diverges from the RFC 8785 reference implementation in edge cases, causing hash chain mismatches for payloads containing those edge-case values.
findings.recommendation: Pin to a specific patch version in Cargo.toml (e.g., '=0.2.1') and track upstream releases. Subscribe to the crate's issue tracker for RFC 8785 conformance updates. Ensure the official RFC 8785 test vectors pass on every dependency update.
findings.confidence_reason: Version pinning concern is operational rather than immediately exploitable. CLAUDE.md lists serde-json-canonicalizer as a monitored dependency.

findings.title: Circuit breaker resets silently on LRU eviction — protection gap after cache eviction
findings.description: When a DID resolver cache entry is evicted from the LRU, the associated circuit breaker state is also lost. An attacker who triggers sufficient LRU evictions can effectively reset the circuit breaker for any DID, bypassing the 5-failure/60s-cooldown protection.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker submits requests with 10001 distinct DIDs to fill and overflow the 10000-entry LRU. The oldest entry's circuit breaker (which was open due to previous failures) is evicted. The attacker can now re-trigger did:web fetches for the evicted DID despite it having been blocked.
findings.recommendation: Maintain circuit breaker state in a separate structure from the LRU cache, with its own bounded store keyed by DID. Circuit breaker entries should have a TTL (e.g., 2 * cooldown period) but should not be evicted by LRU pressure alone.
findings.confidence_reason: The LRU eviction circuit breaker reset is a real but low-likelihood attack. Requires controlling a large number of distinct DIDs.

findings.title: Half-open circuit breaker allows concurrent probes — thundering herd on recovery
findings.description: When the circuit breaker enters half-open state (allowing one probe request), concurrent requests may all simultaneously be allowed through before the probe result is recorded. This creates a thundering herd on recovery — all concurrent requests probe the failing endpoint simultaneously rather than a single probe test.
findings.exploit_scenario: 100 concurrent requests arrive during the circuit half-open window. All 100 probe the did:web endpoint simultaneously. If the endpoint is still failing, all 100 fail, but only one failure is needed to re-open the circuit — the other 99 attempts waste resources.
findings.recommendation: Use an atomic compare-and-swap to ensure only one goroutine transitions from half-open to probing at a time. Other goroutines in the half-open window should wait for the probe result.
findings.confidence_reason: Thundering herd on circuit recovery is a known pattern. Low severity — the worst outcome is wasted recovery probes, not a security bypass.

findings.title: No failed-authentication audit log for admin revocation endpoint
findings.description: Failed authentication attempts against /admin/revoke are rejected but not logged as a security event. Without a failed-auth audit log, detecting token brute-force attempts requires inferring from HTTP 401 response metrics alone, with no correlation to the source IP or timing pattern.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker brute-forces /admin/revoke at the rate limit. Without failed-auth logging, the attack is invisible in the audit log. An operator reviewing logs would see only metrics, not a named security event with source IP, timestamp, and attempted token hash.
findings.recommendation: Add slog.Warn('admin auth failed', 'ip', clientIP, 'ua', userAgent) on every 401 from /admin/revoke. Include a truncated (not full) hash of the attempted token for correlation without leaking the secret. Emit a metrics counter admin_auth_failures_total with IP label.
findings.confidence_reason: Audit logging gap. Low severity as exploiting the admin endpoint also requires the rate-limiting gap (F-031) to be absent.

findings.title: splitn(4, '.') latent off-by-one — inconsistent with similar JWT split code
findings.description: The Rust JWT splitting code uses splitn(4, '.') but validates length == 3, which is correct (splitn(4) produces at most 4 parts, so len == 3 means exactly 3 dot-separated segments). However, using splitn(3) would be clearer and semantically correct: it returns exactly 3 parts for a valid JWT and fails cleanly for inputs with more than 2 dots. The current code is correct but the n=4 choice is surprising.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct exploit. A future maintainer who changes the validation or the split count could introduce a parsing inconsistency. Maintenance risk only.
findings.recommendation: Change splitn(4, '.') to splitn(3, '.') and validate len == 3. This makes the intent clearer: a valid JWT has exactly 2 dots. Add a comment explaining why splitn(3) is used.
findings.confidence_reason: Code quality observation. No exploitable condition in current code.
